content: Cough is a common concern for parents and a significant reason for outpatient visits. It can negatively affect the quality of life, cause anxiety, and disrupt sleep for both children and their parents. Honey has historically been used as a remedy to alleviate cough symptoms. This review updates previous evaluations conducted in 2010, 2012, and 2014, focusing on the effectiveness of honey for treating acute cough in children in outpatient settings. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of honey in managing acute cough in children aged 12 months to 18 years. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing honey alone or in combination with antibiotics against no treatment, placebo, honey-based cough syrups, or other over-the-counter cough medications. The studies were conducted in ambulatory settings. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, EBSCO, Web of Science, and LILACS, with additional searches in ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trial Registry Platform. The search period extended up to February 2018. However, AMED and CAB Abstracts were not included in this update due to lack of institutional access. Six randomized controlled trials involving 899 children were included in the review, with three new studies (331 children) added in this update. The studies compared honey with various treatments, including dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, salbutamol, bromelin (an enzyme derived from the pineapple family), no treatment, and placebo. The methodological quality of the studies varied, with some studies showing high risk of performance and detection bias, and others having unclear risks of attrition or other biases. Five studies used 7-point Likert scales to measure cough symptom relief, while one study used an unclear 5-point scale. In all cases, lower scores indicated better symptom relief. The results showed that honey probably reduces cough frequency more effectively than no treatment or placebo. Specifically, using a 7-point Likert scale, honey demonstrated a mean difference (MD) of -1.05 (95% confidence interval [CI] -1.48 to -0.62) compared to no treatment, and an MD of -1.62 (95% CI -3.02 to -0.22) compared to placebo. Both findings were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. When compared to dextromethorphan, honey may have a similar effect in reducing cough frequency, with an MD of -0.07 (95% CI -1.07 to 0.94), though the evidence was of low certainty. Honey may be more effective than diphenhydramine in reducing cough frequency, with an MD of -0.57 (95% CI -0.90 to -0.24), based on low-certainty evidence. Honey was also found to be more effective than placebo or salbutamol in relieving cough symptoms when used for up to three days. However, beyond three days, honey showed no significant advantage over salbutamol or placebo in reducing cough severity, bothersome cough, or the impact of cough on sleep for children and their parents. In one study using a 5-point cough scale, there was likely little or no difference between honey and bromelin mixed with honey in reducing cough frequency and severity. Adverse events were reported in some cases. Seven children (9.3%) treated with honey experienced nervousness, insomnia, or hyperactivity, compared to two children (2.7%) treated with dextromethorphan. The risk ratio (RR) for these events was 2.94 (95% CI 0.74 to 11.71), based on low-certainty evidence. In the diphenhydramine group, three children (7.5%) experienced somnolence, with an RR of 0.14 (95% CI 0.01 to 2.68). Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported by 34 children (12%) in the honey group and 13 children (11%) in the placebo group, with an RR of 1.91 (95% CI 1.12 to 3.24). Four children treated with salbutamol developed rashes, compared to one child in the honey group, with an RR of 0.19 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.63). No adverse events were reported in the no-treatment group. In conclusion, honey likely provides greater relief of cough symptoms compared to no treatment, diphenhydramine, and placebo, but it may have little or no difference in effect compared to dextromethorphan. Honey probably reduces cough duration more effectively than placebo and salbutamol. However, the evidence is not strong enough to definitively recommend honey as a treatment for acute cough in children. Most children in the studies received treatment for only one night, which limits the generalizability of the findings. There was no significant difference in the occurrence of adverse events between the honey and control groups.
